item.title: A Bull Market, Fueled by Pikachu, Charizard and Nostalgia
item.description:
Scott Pratte turned his boyhood hobby into his livelihood. But he doesn’t usually tell people he’s a Pokémon card collector.

In conversations, he is vague about what he does for a living, saying his business involves collectibles or investments.

“I wouldn’t want to share numbers on the record,” Mr. Pratte, 39, said in an interview, though he noted that the past few years have been “million-dollar years in earnings.”

Pokémon originated as a pair of video games released in Japan for Nintendo’s Game Boy console in 1996. The franchise expanded to include a trading card game, released the same year, which came to the United States in 1999. That’s when Mr. Pratte and others first marveled at the artwork, swapped cards on playgrounds and obsessed over completing sets they shrouded in plastic sleeves in protective binders.

As Pokémon has grown — on its 30th anniversary, the franchise now spans TV shows and films, all manner of merchandise and a stable of more than 1,000 “pocket monsters” — the cards have skyrocketed in value.

Logan Paul, a social media influencer and professional wrestler, sold a rare Pikachu Illustrator card from 1998 at an auction in February for a record $16.5 million. Rarity and nostalgia help drive prices, collectors say, as well as the grading of the cards by authentication companies.

“It is very similar to trading stocks,” Mr. Pratte said. “I think Pikachu and the cute little Pokémon on the cards distract from how competitive and cutthroat it can be.”

What started as a childhood hobby ballooned into a lucrative career because “I genuinely like them,” he said of the cards.

As their value increases, he finds it harder to associate the cards with the same magical memories of his youth — but he understands their enduring appeal.

“Certain cards have become so valuable that you have to sell them,” Mr. Pratte said. “We wouldn’t be able to sell cards for these prices if that emotional value didn’t exist.”

Gary Haase, known online as King Pokémon, was a middle-aged father when he started collecting as a way to bond with his sons. They enjoyed playing the card game and relished opening packs. One of the boys, he recalled, once fell asleep clutching a card featuring the hugely popular character Charizard.

When his children became teenagers and started finding girls more interesting than Pokémon, Mr. Haase kept up with the hobby. As a lifelong collector of sports cards and other items, he understood the value of keeping the cards in mint condition.

Guinness World Records recognizes him as owning the most valuable Pokémon card collection in the world. Part of Mr. Haase’s trove, including multiple rare Charizard cards, is listed on eBay for $59 million.

But he has no intention of actually selling. Ten years ago he put it up for $15 million to “just show it off so people can see it and enjoy it,” he said.

As Pokémon card values rise, he keeps the price at what he estimates to be $10 million to $20 million above market value. “I don’t want somebody to hit it and then I’m obligated to sell,” Mr. Haase said.

In Britain, another father of a Pokémon fan continued collecting in the early 2000s after his son outgrew the hobby. At some point, he put the collection in his attic and didn’t think much of it until he saw a local newspaper article about a Pokémon card that had sold at auction for £6,000, or about $8,000.

The man then took his collection to Ewbank’s Auctions in Surrey, a county southwest of London, which had sold the card. A conservative early estimate by the auction house — which said the man had requested anonymity — suggested that his cards could fetch several hundred thousand pounds, said Andrew Ewbank, a partner at Ewbank Auctions.

Leading up to the auction, it seemed as if the collection would top expectations, as interest spiked and people paid visits to inspect the cards while donning white gloves. The cards, auctioned off in sets, ended up selling for £1.5 million, or about $2.1 million, Mr. Ewbank said.

Lee Steinfeld quit his lawyer job in 2017 to be a full-time YouTube personality. As “Leonhart,” he has more than two million subscribers who tune into see him rip into packs with the same delight he had for the cards as a young boy.

“I’m absolutely grateful to be doing what I do, opening up Pokémon cards for a living,” said Mr. Steinfeld, 39, of Dallas. “I can’t believe I’m not tired of this.”

All markets are prone to fluctuation; in fact, The New York Times reported when the bottom fell out of Pokémon cards 25 years ago, at a time when a high of $375 for the rarest cards seems very affordable by current standards. But there are few signs of a slowdown today, when streamers such as Mr. Steinfeld are a common presence at card conventions and the boom in Pokémon cards drives up the broader trading card market.

Reece Felix, 25, an owner of Aloha Card Shop with stores across Hawaii, traces the success of his business to his childhood love for Pokémon. When he was growing up on the Big Island, his mother would take him to a Kmart store to buy cards when he earned good grades.

It’s become more socially acceptable for adults to collect Pokémon cards, he said in a phone interview from Japan, where he was opening another store.

In 2022, his first store in Honolulu was robbed at gunpoint of Pokémon and sports cards worth around $36,000 — a scary memory for Mr. Felix, but one that shows the high stakes involved in the hobby.

The joy that collecting Pokémon cards brings him outweighs his desire to sell them, he said: “I definitely know how to invest in Pokémon cards and I have done so successfully, but my collector brain outweighs my want-to-have-cash brain.”

Kian Golshan started in high school, learning how to turn cards into valuable assets. (He played Pokémon on his Game Boy when he was younger.)

Now, 27, he said he was intent on buying cards that he hoped would appreciate. And they have: One collection he bought in 2020 for about $8,000 is now worth about $200,000 to $300,000, he said.

“Based on all my research, I knew that this was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to purchase it at the time,” said Mr. Golshan, who lives in Southern California. “It was in immaculate condition.”

The Pokémon cards are still mostly a hobby Mr. Golshan, who works in finance.

“It was a combination of a lot of luck and some research from a while ago that ended up paying off, but I would hope people don’t go into debt,” he said.

Rylie Avery is a Pokémon fan who prides herself on not spending a lot of money collecting the cards.

A 24-year-old kindergarten teacher in Jackson, Mich., Ms. Avery says one of her earliest childhood memories is crawling around her older brother’s bedroom and picking cards out of the floorboards. She has always been drawn to the artwork, and enjoys giving cards to students.

Everyday collectors are more driven by emotion than monetary value, she said.

“It’s something they love or find cute and adorable,” she said. “It brings them joy, not just from the money, but just from a love of the game.”

item.title: Democrats Will Wield Enormous Power in Statehouses. What Will They Do?
item.description:
The midterm tsunami that swept Democrats to power in Congress also gave them control of state capitals from Pennsylvania to Nevada where they will be able to wield power swiftly and consequentially, in ways that will impact lives almost immediately.

Democrats will control the governorship and both legislative houses in six new states — Arizona, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Nevada, Michigan and Minnesota — and hold the majority in a dozen new statehouse chambers.

At least 530 legislative seats changed parties across the country, the Democrats’ best showing since the Watergate era and the biggest partisan swing since Republicans gained more than 700 seats and flipped 22 chambers in 2010.

“It is hard to overstate how massive of a political earthquake this was,” said State Representative Oscar De Los Santos, the incoming Arizona House speaker, who at age 33, wasn’t even alive the last time Arizona Democrats held the majority in any legislative chamber.

What comes next could be dramatic.

In Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and Nevada, Democrats want to raise the minimum wage, strengthen unions and pass paid family leave. They will face minimal opposition from powerless Republicans in the minority.

In Georgia and Texas, where Democrats will unexpectedly occupy the governor’s office and control their state houses, Republicans still holding the state senates will face enormous pressure to finally expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act. Wisconsin, one of the few states outside the South that has not expanded Medicaid, could do so quickly.

New Democratic governors will also move to rein in data centers and artificial intelligence.

And in Arizona, Democrats who have not held control of the legislature and governor’s mansion in 60 years, are determined to repeal abortion restrictions and revamp a costly school vouchers program as part of what Mr. De Los Santos called “big, bold initiatives that help working people.”

In a nationalized political environment, media and voter attention have gravitated to the presidency and Congress. But checks, balances, vetoes and filibusters will continue to be the rule in Washington, where government remains divided, even if Democrats will enjoy larger congressional majorities than they’ve seen in years.

The action, instead, might be in the states, where power can be less checked by structure and tradition.

In all, 22 states will have Democratic “trifectas” — a Democratic governor and both chambers of the legislature. Alaska will have a functional trifecta, with the Democratic governor-elect, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, working with a coalition of Democrats, Republicans and independents that he helped assemble.

Tension between centrists and a resurgent left wing are inevitable, but Democratic leaders expressed optimism that at least in the initial rush, they can find consensus.

“It’s just the legislative process,” said Austin Davis, the Pennsylvania lieutenant governor, “which I think will be a lot easier with members of the same party controlling all three branches of government.”

So Mr. De Los Santos said he was consulting with other states with recent experience in flipping chambers, such as Minnesota and Michigan, and ones with strong Democratic majorities, like next-door New Mexico.

Democratic legislators and organizers are also workshopping ideas and taking a page from the American Legislative Exchange Council, which has worked for decades with conservative lawmakers and business interests to draft model legislation.

“There’s just such a tremendous feeling of optimism and also urgency,” said Gaby Goldstein, the founder of State Futures, a network of 900 progressive lawmakers which has organized state officials to push back on President Trump’s mass deportations and other policies. “This is crunchtime between now and January for a lot of the agenda setting.”

The most closely watched new trifecta could be Wisconsin.

Governor-elect David Crowley, a moderate Democrat, will be flanked by a state House and Senate controlled by Democrats for the first time since 2010. At that time, the then-governor, Scott Walker, and his fellow Republicans moved quickly to strip public union bargaining rights; cut income taxes; reduce education funding; expand vouchers for private school tuition; and approve gerrymandered State House and Senate maps that would lock in their power for years.

Though Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat, has served for two terms, he has mostly played goalie, using veto power and attempting to block legislation pushed by Republicans.

Democrats’ memories may well be long. Greta Neubauer, the incoming Assembly speaker, said in an interview this week that she and her Democratic colleagues intended to move quickly. Their initial aim, she said, will be addressing the cost of living by lowering the costs of groceries, gas, health care and child care.

That could mean a bill that expands access to free or reduced-price meals in schools, which would help families have lower grocery costs, or a tax credit for renters and homeowners that essentially lowers property taxes.

“We of course have many other priorities as well — protecting people’s rights and freedoms, strengthening our democracy, building strong schools and creating good jobs,” Ms. Neubauer said.

In an email, Mr. Walker said that the new Democratic leaders “have every right to enact their own agenda.”

But he warned that if they deviated from a focus on cost of living issues, another political backlash could be in store.

“If liberals ignore the will of the people,” he said, “there will be another major shift in the 2028 elections.”

Michigan might be more cautious, said Maggie Mick, a senior vice president at MultiState, a state and local government relations firm. That is in part, she said, because Democrats are cognizant of how they lost their trifecta in 2024 after swinging big on abortion, right-to-work and L.G.B.T.Q. issues.

“They have gone through the whiplash of losing the majority,” she said.

In Pennsylvania, where Democrats captured the State Senate for the first time since the 1990s, whatever Harrisburg does will be viewed through the lens of an anticipated 2028 presidential run by Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat.

With a comfortable majority in the House and a slim one in the state senate, Democrats intend to quickly enact laws that would increase transit funding, more than double the minimum wage, expand the availability of housing, add amendments to the constitution protecting abortion rights and allowing people to seek civil damages for childhood sexual abuse.

Those five items, which Gov. Shapiro has championed, “hit a sweet spot,” said State Representative Mike Schlossberg, a Democrat. “They’re relatively easy to pass, they’re highly popular and they’re incredibly important.”

This list aligns with Mr. Shapiro’s brand as a center-left Democrat. Even if some lawmakers would want to push the agenda further to the left, there is not much room for dissension: the Democrats need every vote of their caucus in the State Senate to pass legislation.

But disagreements are inevitable, said State Senator Nikil Saval, a Democrat and a member of the Democratic Socialists of America.

“Those debates will engage a broad section of the public who felt shut out of politics in Harrisburg until now,” he said.

Beyond that initial list of priorities, some legislation may include bills about the regulation of gambling and marijuana.

Several states are also likely to tackle concerns about utility bills and data centers.

In Georgia, Democrats won the governor’s office and the state House of Representatives, as well as a majority for the first time in decades on the Georgia Public Service Commission, which regulates utilities.

State Senator Chuck Hufstetler, a Republican who chairs his chamber’s finance committee, wanted to create a consumer watchdog office and require that data centers pay more, only to be blocked by his own party’s leaders. He plans to introduce new bills in 2027.

“I do see a bipartisan path forward,” he texted last week, while on a trip to China with a U.S. delegation looking at utilities and energy infrastructure.

Curbing health care costs is likely to be a common denominator in many states. In an interview with The New York Times, Georgia’s governor-elect, Keisha Lance Bottoms, said she was already drafting a budget that assumes the state will expand Medicaid, bringing government-funded health insurance to more middle-class Georgians — if the narrowly controlled Republican Senate goes along.

Ms. Goldstein, of State Futures, anticipated a renewed push in several states to prohibit medical debt from being included in credit reports. States could also band together to purchase prescription drugs in bulk to reduce costs.

Another priority is abortion access, said Bella Pori, associate director of state policy for Reproductive Freedom for All.

She pointed to North Carolina, where Democrats will control the House and likely end up just shy of controlling the Senate. Over the last decade, Republicans have dramatically increased funding to crisis pregnancy centers, which critics say are anti-abortion fronts. Such centers receive more than $10 million a year in the state.

Next year, Democrats may propose that there be no funding or less funding.

She also pointed to Arizona, where Democrats are likely to enact a shield law protecting providers and out-of-state patients, and also to repeal abortion restrictions.

At a news conference Tuesday at the state capitol in Phoenix, Democratic leaders said they wanted to increase funding for public schools, which have been strained by a program supplying vouchers for private schools, often to Arizonans who already had their children in those schools. They also want to further protect Arizona’s dwindling supply of groundwater, said Priya Sundareshan, the State Senate’s president-elect.

“Our job now is to make sure that you feel the difference at your kitchen table, in your kids’ classrooms and in your community,” she said.

Gov. Katie Hobbs marveled at how, 15 years ago, as a member of state legislature, she had so few Democratic colleagues that they called themselves the One Pizza Caucus, because a single pie could feed them all.

“We’re going to need a lot more pizzas,” she said.

item.title: Raman Has Lots of Plans. Los Angeles Has Lots of Obstacles.
item.description:
A month before Nithya Raman swept to victory as Los Angeles’s next mayor, she announced what she would do in her first 100 days if she won.

The audience was scant — the speech had somehow been scheduled outside during the dinner hour on a Sunday in searing heat with the Dodgers at home in the playoffs. Still, her most ardent fans gathered, sweltering, around her. If they expected a fire-breathing leftist manifesto from their candidate, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, they were wrong.

Ms. Raman, a 45-year-old member of the Los Angeles City Council with a master’s degree in urban planning, didn’t talk about defunding police, removing the private sector from housing construction or other items from a D.S.A. wish list. Rather, she outlined a near future of mapping out trouble spots and restructuring org charts. She would launch dashboards and audits, she said, and base performance evaluations on results and metrics. In her pursuit of a more livable city, she would drill down to a “nitty-gritty” so granular that it would “make your eyes glaze over.”

“In just one century, Los Angeles built itself into a global metropolis, the gateway to the Pacific, a center of ingenuity and invention, and the cultural capital of the entire planet,” Ms. Raman exhorted. “Don’t tell me the city of Los Angeles can’t fix a streetlight!”

The speech was a striking shift in a deep-blue city that has spent the past decade consumed with big-picture crises: Covid-19. Natural disasters. Clashes with the Trump administration, particularly over federal immigration enforcement. In many ways, political experts say, the election Ms. Raman won two weeks ago was a plea for a way back to normal.

“The issue in this election was not left versus right, but change versus the same,” said Zev Yaroslavsky, the director of the Los Angeles Initiative at the University of California, Los Angeles, and a longtime civic leader. “It was broken versus fixed.”

What Ms. Raman will be able to “fix” in Los Angeles is an open question. Power to enact policy in the city is diffuse. The mayor represents only about 4 million of the 10 million residents of Los Angeles County. Local authority is shared not only with the 15-member City Council but also with the county Board of Supervisors, which controls most social service spending.

In two years, a shift in governance that voters approved in 2024 will turn the top county government job into an elective office, effectively installing a new, more powerful countywide leader to rival Ms. Raman.

The city’s budget — roughly $13 billion not counting the city’s water and power department and airport — has been stretched thin, in part by commitments made under Karen Bass, the current mayor. The police union, which heavily backed Ms. Bass for re-election, received significant raises during her tenure, constraining the amount of money that Ms. Raman will have for projects.

Downtown business interests, which backed Ms. Bass as well, won an overhaul of the city convention center that is projected to siphon more than $100 million annually from the city’s general fund in debt service for the next three decades. The Olympics, typically a huge financial risk for the host city, are coming to town in 2028.

In interviews, Ms. Raman’s supporters and local political experts predicted that she will draw from a new generation of Democratic big-city mayors to push her agenda. They include the democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani in New York, political centrists like Daniel Lurie in San Francisco and progressive technocrats like Michelle Wu in Boston.

Like Mr. Lurie, her advisers say, she intends to rebrand her embattled city as a comeback story. Like Mr. Mamdani, she plans to improve the housing supply and tenant protections. Like Ms. Wu, she is likely to rely heavily on data and community input. Like all three, they add, her approach is less likely to be ideological than pragmatic.

“There has been a wave in our way of thinking about mayors,” said Megan Mullin, a professor of public affairs at the University of California, Los Angeles. “A mayor can be a visionary, or a power broker, or a political boss, or a coalition builder. This is an idea of the mayor as the manager of a big operation that delivers services that make our lives possible in a city — the mayor as C.E.O.”

Historically, politics in sprawling Los Angeles have been driven by single-family homeowners who commute by freeway. But precinct-level data that has emerged in the vote for mayor shows that Ms. Raman was carried into office amid surging turnout by young voters and Latinos, who are more likely to rent and rely on public transit.

“A city that works” was her slogan, but rent control laws for tenants and dedicated lanes on the streets for bicycle enthusiasts and bus riders are not necessarily appealing to older property owners and freeway commuters, said Mike Bonin, executive director of the Pat Brown Institute for Public Affairs at Cal State Los Angeles.

“It’s a big shift, and it’s largely generationally driven,” Mr. Bonin said. “Where the two groups do coincide is just on this sense that the city is broken and let’s clean it up.”

Ms. Raman, 45, who joined the City Council six years ago in the aftermath of the George Floyd protests, has favored left-leaning policy goals like strong rent regulations, denser housing near public transit and a less militarized approach to policing. At the time, she was endorsed by the D.S.A., the movement that later would help elect Mr. Mamdani.

She has since had a fraught relationship with the organization. During her campaign, she vowed to regard it as just one part of her governing coalition, though the movement clearly influenced her pledge to replace the police chief.

Ms. Raman has said she will reorganize lines of authority in the mayor’s office, designating a “chief operating officer” and a “chief financial officer” to help her manage the dozens of department heads in the city who answer to the mayor but, in practice, have often operated with scant oversight.

She also has promised to appoint a “recovery czar” for Pacific Palisades, where rebuilding from the 2025 wildfires has been sluggish; a “nightlife czar” to revive the city’s restaurant scene and cultural districts; a Hollywood liaison to speed permitting and market local production; an advocate for renters to run an “office of tenant protections”; and an “experienced financial executive” to oversee city spending on the 2028 Olympics, which could cost Los Angeles hundreds of millions of dollars if there are overruns.

In concert with the city controller, Kenneth Mejia, a D.S.A.-aligned progressive, she has pledged to “launch tools in which you can see our progress, our successes, and our failures in real time.”

In that vein, she has said she will introduce public monitoring of the police department to ensure that it follows the city’s edicts against using local officers to conduct federal immigration enforcement.

She will also publicly audit spending on homelessness, a priority for Ms. Bass, who used city funds for motel rooms to address rampant street encampments after the pandemic. Ms. Raman’s plan is to use time-limited housing vouchers, which are less expensive but depend on a steady supply of vacant apartments and willing landlords.

She has also indicated that she will lean into her training as an urban planner, just as Ms. Bass leaned into hers as a physician assistant and lawmaker. To create urgency around the city’s chronic maintenance issues, Ms. Raman has pledged to publicly map broken streetlights and publish deadlines to repair them. To hasten building, she said, she will put housing permits on a “shot clock” to cut red tape.

Mike Murphy, a Republican political consultant who has advised past mayoral candidates in Los Angeles, said that Ms. Raman will have her work cut out for her. Aside from financial constraints, she will be working with a City Council whose members all declined to endorse her, though they congratulated her at a council meeting last week.

“She’s going to need a big coalition to make any changes, because politically in L.A., they’re so hard,” said Mr. Murphy. “Will she start firing police chiefs and be a justice warrior? Or will she widen her appeal so she can actually do things? D.S.A., not D.S.A.? It’s an open question. But it’s time for action now.”

item.title: Judge Could Set New Trial Date for Lindsay Clancy
item.description:
A judge could set a new trial date as soon as Monday for Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman whose first trial for the deaths of her three young children ended with a deadlocked jury.

Prosecutors have not yet said whether they plan to retry Ms. Clancy on first-degree murder charges, lesser charges or at all. But Judge William Sullivan indicated at a hearing earlier this month that he intends to choose a tentative start date for a second trial, and that he may do so at a 10 a.m. hearing on Monday in Plymouth Superior Court.

Jurors at Ms. Clancy’s first trial were unable to break their 11-1 deadlock after nearly 40 hours of deliberations, and the judge declared a mistrial on Sept. 2. If prosecutors reduce the charges to second-degree murder or manslaughter, Ms. Clancy could avoid a second jury trial and have her fate decided by a judge instead.

Judge Sullivan dismissed several motions by Ms. Clancy’s lawyers last week, including one that argued for the dismissal of the charges. Her lawyers have asserted that any retrial would constitute double jeopardy because the mistrial could have been avoided if the judge had dug deeper into the conduct of the lone juror who voted to convict.

The defense team said in its motion that if the judge had investigated further, he might have found grounds for dismissing that juror and replacing him with an alternate.

In his ruling, Judge Sullivan found that such an inquiry would have been “impermissibly coercive,” given the lack of evidence that the juror had done anything wrong. Judge Sullivan also dismissed a defense motion arguing for further investigation of the holdout juror.

Kevin Reddington, the lawyer for Ms. Clancy, had argued that the juror had failed to disclose information about his own past criminal charges. Heather O’Connor, a lawyer for the juror, has said that he “believed he was truthful” on the juror questionnaire that he filled out during the jury selection process last summer.

Ms. Clancy, 36, has remained in custody at a state hospital since the mistrial. Her trial was televised and lasted for six weeks, attracting an enormous and opinionated audience.

Mr. Reddington had argued during the trial that she was not criminally responsible for killing Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months, because she was experiencing severe postpartum mental illness and hallucinated a voice that ordered her to kill them and herself. After strangling her children, Ms. Clancy cut her wrists and throat and jumped from a window, sustaining spinal injuries that left her paralyzed.

The trial revived a national debate about postpartum mental illness, its treatment and how resulting criminal cases should be treated by the courts. Ms. Clancy’s lawyer focused on her persistent but unsuccessful efforts to find effective mental health care in the months before the killings.

The online furor around the case, and the intense scrutiny and criticism of the jurors after the mistrial, have raised concerns about the prospect of seating another jury for a second trial, given the likely trepidation of prospective jurors.

At the hearing on Nov. 2, Mr. Reddington expressed impatience with prosecutors after they declined to say whether they would try Ms. Clancy again for first-degree murder. Timothy Cruz, the Plymouth district attorney, has pledged to continue seeking justice for the Clancy children, and he is widely seen as an uncompromising prosecutor.

“The ball is in Mr. Cruz’s court,” Mr. Reddington said at the hearing this month.

item.title: ‘Steering Failure’ Likely Caused Tanker’s Collision With Riverboat, N.T.S.B. Says
item.description:
The tanker that struck a docked riverboat carrying nearly 200 people on Friday in New Orleans appeared to have had a “steering failure,” according to initial findings from the National Transportation Safety Board.

It was not immediately clear what that meant or what may have caused it, officials said, emphasizing that the findings were preliminary.

“We purposefully worded it in that way,” Bart Barnum, a senior marine engineer in the N.T.S.B.’s Office of Marine Safety, said during a news conference on Sunday. “It can be many different things. That is something we are investigating very closely.”

Because of “an issue with the steering on board,” Mr. Barnum said, the tanker’s rudder remained in a starboard position, which caused it to veer toward the east bank of the Mississippi River.

Investigators also said they were analyzing the tanker’s voyage data recorder but were not ready to publicly release its information, including the vessel’s speed at the time of the collision.

The tanker, named the Atlantic Asphalt, lost control on Friday and veered into the side of the passenger boat, causing it to capsize at its dock on the river. The crash prompted a wide-scale search-and-rescue operation that ended with all passengers and crew members accounted for, in what Gov. Jeff Landry of Louisiana called “a literal miracle on the Mississippi.”

The American Cruise Lines riverboat, named American Heritage, took about 22 minutes to capsize, John DeLeeuw, a member of the N.T.S.B., said at the news conference on Sunday.

The tanker had 19 crew members and a local pilot on board, Mr. DeLeeuw said. The riverboat had 140 passengers and 50 crew members on board at the time of the crash.

Officials said 32 people were taken to the hospital and one had serious injuries. People clung to the rails and screamed as the riverboat overturned, videos posted online showed.

The riverboat, which had arrived from Natchez, Miss., had been docked for about two hours and was beginning to unload passengers when the tanker struck it, said Kimberly Curth, a spokeswoman for the Port of New Orleans.

item.title: Trump Administration Moves to Close A.I. Chip Loophole Ahead of China Trip
item.description:
The Trump administration said on Monday that it was moving forward with a new rule that would clamp down on China’s ability to access advanced A.I. chips through the use of data centers outside China’s borders.

The rule aims to close what many in Washington see as a loophole that has allowed China to sidestep a Commerce Department ban that prevents Chinese firms from buying the most advanced A.I. chips made by companies like Nvidia. China’s ability to continue accessing the chips by renting them from data centers in Southeast Asian countries and elsewhere has been a focus of contention within the Trump administration.

The new rule establishes restrictions for overseas data centers that supply “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in a small group of high-risk countries, a list that includes China, Russia and Iran. Data centers are also required to perform due diligence on those customers. The provision will “undermine” the ability of companies in those countries from using U.S. chips to train advanced A.I. models, the release said.

It will also require a license to export advanced chips to companies with headquarters in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, which have a higher than normal risk of smuggling, the administration said.

A plan to restrict that loophole comes just days before President Trump is scheduled to travel to China for an economic summit, where he will also meet with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping.

The formerly obscure issue has become more prominent in recent weeks with the revelations about Megaspeed, a Singaporean data center firm created by a woman who had an affair with Jensen Huang, who was ousted as Nvidia’s chief executive last week. U.S. authorities deemed the woman, Alice Huang, to be an asset for Chinese intelligence services, and they are investigating Megaspeed over allegations of smuggling chips to China.

Megaspeed’s business, the operation of data centers in Southeast Asia that remotely serve Chinese clients, is legal. That means Chinese companies that are blocked from buying advanced Nvidia chips directly can simply rent them through other Southeast Asian firms.

Nvidia and its proponents contend that the sales help create jobs in the United States and ensure that companies around the world are reliant on American technology.

But some officials in the Trump administration and in Congress increasingly appear to believe that Chinese access to these data centers has undercut U.S. export controls and allowed China’s artificial intelligence ecosystem to flourish. Some worry this could give Beijing an economic edge, as well as a military one.

In a news release, the Commerce Department said the rule was “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.”

The move would bring America’s rules on remote access of data centers into alignment with its rules on the physical shipment of sensitive American technology, the department said.

Just before leaving office, the Biden administration issued global rules on chip sales, including restrictions on Chinese firms remotely accessing data centers. Trump officials said they would no longer enforce the rules after Mr. Trump won another term, and in May 2025 they officially rescinded the restrictions.

Since then, various draft versions of the rules have gained momentum in the government, only to be shot down by opponents.

In recent months, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the U.S. trade representative, Jamieson Greer, have all pushed to reinstate broad restrictions on data centers, amid concerns about Nvidia’s advanced chips reaching China.

But they faced pushback from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees chip export policy. Mr. Lutnick has pushed for a leaner version of the rules, one that would be less onerous for Nvidia and foreign data centers.

The announcement published Monday said that the new rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council” — both parts of the administration that have pushed for more stringent rules.

It remains to be seen whether the new rules will trigger blowback from China. Mr. Trump heads to Asia this week and arrives in China on Wednesday for meetings that are expected to address the war in Iran, nuclear nonproliferation and trade.

In a telephone briefing on Friday, a senior administration official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity as part of the ground rules of the call, said the administration had been discussing potential measures on remote access and did not expect countermeasures from China in response. The moves would close loopholes in existing measures to counteract both smuggling and remote access of data centers, and the Chinese have stated publicly that they are not involved with smuggling, the official said.

Another senior administration official on the call said the situation with Nvidia would not have any bearing on the trip. Export controls are national security matters and are not up for negotiation with the Chinese, the official said.

item.title: Trump Says He’s Open to Reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia Chief
item.description:
President Trump said on Monday that he was open to seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as the head of Nvidia, his latest public expression of support for the executive who resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman whom U.S. officials had identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

“I would not mind; I would not mind that,” Mr. Trump told reporters on the South Lawn of the White House as he departed for a dayslong trip to Asia, including a stop in China.

“I think he learned a big lesson — I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another,” he added.

The president cast doubt on whether Alice Huang, the woman with whom Mr. Huang had a relationship, was actually a spy.

“I don’t know that she is a spy,” Mr. Trump said. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy. I don’t know that she was a spy at all.”

The president has repeatedly defended Mr. Huang since the revelations.

Last week, Mr. Trump called Mr. Huang before he stepped down and urged him to keep fighting for his job, The New York Times reported.

Mr. Trump was warned at least twice about Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang, who intelligence agencies concluded had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, The Times has reported. The first warning was late last year, and the second was in the spring.

But the president has continued to express sympathy for Mr. Huang. He told reporters last week that he was concerned with how the technology executive was holding up amid the controversy.

“I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right,” Mr. Trump said then, adding: “I believe he’s suffering greatly. I read his statement, and I believe he’s suffering greatly. More so because of his family, his wife who he loves and his family, but he is definitely suffering.”

item.title: Challenging Consensus, Scientist Says Photos Show Epstein Was Killed
item.description:
Michael Freeman says he had one thought when he first saw a photo from Jeffrey Epstein’s autopsy: “Wait a minute, that doesn’t look like a hanging mark.”

The noose had not left a smooth, consistent line on Mr. Epstein’s neck that slanted to a peak, as in a textbook hanging. Instead, the mark was deep, ragged and branched into a Y-shape on one side.

Dr. Freeman, a forensic scientist who studies bias and error in death investigations, spent a year examining Mr. Epstein’s autopsy file, which was given to him by the dead man’s brother.

He is seeking to publish his findings in a peer-reviewed journal, but has been rejected so far. On Monday he was presenting them at the Middle Temple, a London legal society, arguing that Mr. Epstein’s injuries are most plausibly explained by homicidal strangulation. He is also asserting that injuries on the body suggest there was a struggle, contrary to the medical examiner’s findings.

The totality of the circumstances surrounding Jeffrey Epstein’s death in a federal detention center in 2019 points overwhelmingly to suicide, and several investigations have failed to produce evidence that anyone other than Mr. Epstein had a hand in it. Dr. Freeman’s analysis, parts of which he floated in a New York Times investigation earlier this year, may rekindle long-smoldering debates about his death.

Forensic pathologists who have seen some of the autopsy photos, though not the entire set, have agreed that the mark on Mr. Epstein’s neck was atypical for a hanging. Some of those experts said the images could still be consistent with suicide, but they cautioned that the injuries alone could not tell the full story, and that a cascade of institutional failures would make it difficult to ever conclusively determine what happened.

The New York City medical examiner’s office, which performed the autopsy, said this week that it “stands by its determination” of suicide.

Much information that medical examiners would normally use to determine a cause of death was unavailable; the examiner was not permitted to inspect the cell, for example. That has left the autopsy photographs as some of the only concrete evidence.

After being asked by a journalist to look at the hanging mark, Dr. Freeman asked Jeffrey Epstein’s brother, Mark, whether he could see the complete file. As next of kin, Mark Epstein was one of the few people who had access to the autopsy. He shared the file with Dr. Freeman last November.

Mark Epstein said in an interview last week that he had also shown the materials to other experts who had asked to see them — but whom he declined to name — and that the results had been inconclusive. “They were all hemming and hawing,” he said.

Shortly before Monday’s talk, Mr. Epstein posted the autopsy photos online for all to see.

Dr. Freeman said in an interview that he had no idea who might have killed Mr. Epstein, nor did he care. He was focused only on what he called oversights in the death investigation and autopsy report. “All I’m interested in is, how did this get so sideways?” he said.

Jeffrey Epstein, a wealthy financier and convicted sex offender, is far from a typical subject for Dr. Freeman. As a consultant and scholar, he has argued that medical examiners too often ignore the most plausible cause of death in favor of one that excuses deadly force by the police or reinforces racial stereotypes.

He is not a board-certified forensic pathologist, the highest credential for medical examiners in the United States, but he has doctorates in epidemiology and forensic medicine and teaches forensic medicine at two universities. Dr. Freeman, an American, is also a fellow of the Faculty of Forensic & Legal Medicine at the Royal College of Physicians in the United Kingdom and the editor of its journal.

In one case, Dr. Freeman argued on behalf of a Black teenager charged with murder in Mississippi after a stillbirth, after tests found trace amounts of a cocaine byproduct in the baby’s blood. The umbilical cord had been wrapped around the infant’s neck, and the state had the country’s highest infant mortality rate. The charges were dropped.

In 2020, Dr. Freeman co-wrote a landmark metastudy on excited delirium, a term often used to explain deaths in police custody. His methodology and conclusions were hotly disputed, but they propelled a widespread rejection of excited delirium as a valid diagnosis or cause of death.

More recently, he consulted in the prosecution of a police officer who killed George Floyd in Minneapolis, using statistical probability to counter defense claims that drug abuse or heart disease had caused Mr. Floyd’s death. Dr. Freeman was also part of a panel of experts that identified dozens of deaths in police custody in Maryland that had been misclassified as natural or accidental.

Forensic pathology is sometimes said to be more art than science, and disagreements among experts are common. Medical examiners point out that they must defend their opinions in court, but Dr. Freeman is among critics who have complained that there are too few safeguards against bias and error.

For his Epstein investigation, he teamed up with two other skeptics, Itiel Dror, a cognitive neuroscientist whose real-world experiments have repeatedly embarrassed forensic practitioners, and Anders Eriksson, a forensic pathologist who led a Swedish government review concluding that “shaken baby” prosecutions had been based on flawed reasoning.

They are continuing to seek a publisher for their analysis. In the meantime, Dr. Freeman prepared his talk on Monday, which received a flurry of advance news coverage.

The talk was to be held at the University College of London, where reservations quickly reached capacity. But on Sunday, the school suddenly announced that it would not take place, citing “wellbeing implications for our students.” The talk was moved to the Middle Temple and those planning to attend were told they would have to watch it online.

In 2019, the medical examiner who performed the autopsy, Dr. Kristin Roman, faced limitations. There were no photos of Mr. Epstein hanging or with the strip of cloth around his neck. The piece of cloth sent to the medical examiner was not the one that had been used as a noose. The prison employee who found the body initially declined to speak to authorities.

Still, Dr. Roman told federal investigators that she had no doubt it was a suicide. There were no signs of a struggle and the body was “pristine,” she told them, with no bruises and no debris under the fingernails.

“This doesn’t look anything like a strangulation,” she said in a statement she gave to federal authorities.

Dr. Roman has since retired from the medical examiner’s office.

When the jail employee who found the body finally spoke with investigators two years after the fact, he recalled that Mr. Epstein’s rear end had been suspended about an inch off the floor.

Dr. Freeman used the employee’s description to reconstruct the hanging, creating 3-D computer models based on Mr. Epstein’s physique and the autopsy photos. He then used illustrations to argue that strangulation from behind was a better explanation for Mr. Epstein’s injuries, including fingernail marks above the ligature line, an abrasion at the base of the neck, and a deep, fresh hemorrhage in the left shoulder muscle.

He faulted the medical examiner for not testing Mr. Epstein’s fingernails for DNA.

Colleagues are welcome to dispute his findings, Dr. Freeman said in an interview.

“It should be, ‘Here’s my work. You do the calculations, you do the math, you take a look at it,’” Dr. Freeman said. “If you agree, great. If you don’t — tell me where I went wrong.’”

If you are having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or go to SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for a list of additional resources.

item.title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Bid to Revive University Research Cuts
item.description:
The Supreme Court on Monday rejected a request from the Trump administration seeking to revive cuts to tens of millions of dollars in research grants to the University of California.

The court’s rejection of the case leaves in place a lower-court ruling that found the Trump administration had most likely violated the First Amendment when it terminated the grants over perceived connections to diversity initiatives.

The announcement by the justices came on a routine orders list and gave no reasoning, as is typical. No dissents were noted.

The decision was a blow to President Trump’s pressure campaign against one of the country’s largest and most prestigious public university systems. The University of California has been a major focus of the president’s critiques of the country’s universities for much of his second term. The 10-campus system has about 560,000 students and employees and receives about $17 billion in federal funding each year.

Matthew J. Tragesser, a Justice Department spokesman, said in a statement that the administration would continue its court fight to cancel the federal research grants and advocate “the executive branch’s lawful authority to administer federal funding programs.”

Erwin Chemerinsky, the dean of the law school at the University of California, Berkeley, who argued on behalf of the researchers, said he was “obviously delighted” that the justices had declined to hear the case and that courts had upheld that “the government cannot cut off grants based on the perceived viewpoint of the research.”

Rachel Zaentz, a spokeswoman for the University of California, said in a statement that the decision “preserves an important victory for the U.C. researchers whose critical work and federal grants were targeted.” She added that it supported “the principle that research funding decisions should be based on merit, not politics.”

In early 2025, three federal agencies terminated grants awarded to researchers in the university system, citing executive orders issued by Mr. Trump. Six researchers from the University of California sued to challenge the cancellations. They had received multiyear research grants from the Environmental Protection Agency, the National Science Foundation and the National Endowment for the Humanities that the administration said it would be canceling.

In May, a three-judge panel from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit concluded that “because the agencies’ termination of grants was aimed at the suppression of viewpoints with which the government disagrees,” the cancellation “likely violates the First Amendment.”

The Trump administration then asked the Supreme Court to weigh in, arguing that the agencies’ decision to terminate the grants represented the sort of ordinary policy shifts of a new administration.

In urging the justices to take the case, Solicitor General D. John Sauer asserted that “changes in administration invariably bring changes in policy and spending priorities” and that “presidents often direct agencies to review and terminate grants that no longer reflect the government’s priorities.”

Lawyers for the researchers pushed back, claiming that the administration had violated the First Amendment by “terminating already awarded grants to faculty and researchers at the University of California based on a perception of the viewpoint expressed in their research.”

In a brief to the justices, the lawyers asserted that federal agencies had identified grant proposals with “what they regarded as ‘dangerous ideas’ based on keywords in their titles and then abruptly cut off their funding.”

Federal agencies had explained in court filings in the case that they had used keywords related to diversity, gender and vaccine hesitancy, among other search terms, to determine whether research grants might collide with policy aims of the Trump administration.

item.title: Chase Bank Reports ‘Technical Issue’ Disrupting Transactions
item.description:
Chase Bank, which serves more than 86 million customers at 5,000 branches across the United States, reported that it was having trouble processing transactions on Monday.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” the bank said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”

A Chase spokeswoman, Meghan Durant, said the bank was not having a “cyber issue.”

“We have no indication of bad actors,” she said.

Some Chase Bank customers reported on social media that they were unable to use their A.T.M. cards or complete transactions at branches on Monday.

Customers at several other major banks, including Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Bank of America, also reported problems on Monday, according to Downdetector.com, a website that tracks user reports of outages. Users also reported issues with the online payment platform Zelle.

U.S. Bank said in a statement that its “systems are not directly impacted.”

“However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays,” it said.

Zelle said it was “not down.”

“Zelle is operating as it should,” it said in a statement, which noted that customers who use the platform access their money through their own bank accounts. “An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers,” it said.

Wells Fargo and Bank of America did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The banking issues were reported days after a global outage at Microsoft disrupted communications and work at schools, government agencies, hospitals and offices around the world. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop after outdated air traffic communications equipment became overloaded and began to fail, officials said.

There was no indication that the bank issues on Monday were related to the outages at Microsoft. But the recent F.A.A. ground stop, which was related to an equipment problem with federal systems, added to the sense of gloom in social media chatter about troubles with modern technology.

The Microsoft outage, which started Thursday and was resolved on Saturday, affected some of its most popular products, including the email manager Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Teams and the artificial intelligence assistant Copilot. Microsoft said the outage had been caused by a “technical issue” and not a cyberattack or A.I. agent.

The F.A.A. ground stop, which was lifted hours after it was issued on Friday, created a cascade of flight delays and cancellations that continued over the weekend. Government officials attributed the disarray to a routine router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark. Workers also noticed a second unspecified issue at a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas.

item.title: Bessent Takes Hawkish Turn in White House Debate on China
item.description:
President Trump heads to Asia on Monday for high-stakes meetings with foreign leaders aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine and smoothing over trade frictions with China. But the most tense meeting could take place aboard Air Force One.

Sequestered together on the journey across the world will be Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, whose long-running rivalry has recently spilled into the open.

Mr. Lutnick is under fire for slow-walking several measures aimed at clamping down on the supply of Nvidia chips to foreign data centers that serve Chinese clients. The controversy has put Mr. Lutnick at odds with Mr. Bessent, who has increasingly taken a hard line on China. While Mr. Lutnick has pushed for policies more favorable to Nvidia, Mr. Bessent has played the foil, going so far as to call for a dramatic shake-up of the company’s leadership.

The Treasury secretary traditionally manages America’s economic relationship with China. After spending much of last year trying to de-escalate tension between the world’s two largest economies over tariffs, Mr. Bessent has taken a more hawkish stance this year amid growing concern over the artificial intelligence race with China and risks that rogue Chinese A.I. technology could pose to the U.S. economy.

The internal clash over China policy has echoes of Mr. Trump’s first term, when the president’s economic advisers regularly argued about how forcefully to confront China over its trade practices. After Mr. Trump imposed steep tariffs on Chinese imports last year, Mr. Bessent called for de-escalation and helped broker a trade truce that stabilized the global economy.

But in recent months, the Trump administration has been frustrated that China has not lived up to its commitments for purchases of American farm products and to accelerate exports of its critical minerals, which are needed for making high-tech electronics and military equipment.

In a call with Vice Premier He Lifeng of China this month, the Treasury Department said, Mr. Bessent “raised concerns about recent Chinese actions” related to the two nations’ agreement and that “continued progress depends on concrete results.”

Michael Pillsbury, a China scholar at the right-leaning Heritage Foundation who advised Mr. Trump during his first term, said that Mr. Bessent’s hawkish turn when it comes to technology exports is part of a broader acknowledgment that tariffs and sanctions are not providing the United States with enough economic leverage when dealing with China.

“It’s the realization that the original plan or hope with China is not working,” Mr. Pillsbury said, adding that Mr. Bessent was being innovative in the “quest for leverage.”

This month the divide over China policy spilled into public view, after Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was revealed to be having an affair with a woman who led a Singaporean data center firm known as Megaspeed. U.S. intelligence believes the woman is a Chinese intelligence asset. The company is under investigation for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

Megaspeed said in a statement that it conducts legitimate and lawful business, and designs its operations to comply with all laws.

When he was asked last week about the U.S. government’s failure to sanction Megaspeed, Mr. Bessent took the unusual step of declaring that he and other officials had long been pushing for action and placed blame on Mr. Lutnick.

“Commerce has the pen,” Mr. Bessent told CNBC. “You will have to ask them about their internal processes.”

On Sunday, Mr. Bessent continued to exert pressure on Nvidia and called on the company to explain itself.

“I want to keep coming back to, what was the culture at Nvidia and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” Mr. Bessent told Fox News.

In 2025, Mr. Lutnick rolled out several aggressive measures on U.S. technology exports, which prompted Beijing to take countermeasures that stopped the flow of critical minerals to the United States. He has since taken a more cautious stance and warned that broad rules regulating overseas data centers could upset America’s relationship with China and other countries.

On Monday, after months of fierce internal debate, the Commerce Department issued a sweeping rule that will crack down on Chinese companies that have been remotely accessing advanced A.I. chips through data centers in Southeast Asia.

Mr. Lutnick had proposed a softer version that would have had less impact on Nvidia, whose chips are used in overseas data centers. But Mr. Bessent and others in the administration wanted a stronger provision that would clamp down on Chinese access to A.I. computing power.

The Commerce Department, which has authority over the topic, ultimately conceded and published a stronger rule on Monday. But officials drafting the release made clear that it wasn’t their idea.

A news release issued by the Commerce Department said that the new rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council” — agencies that have both pushed for more stringent rules.

Christopher Padilla, a former Commerce Department official in the Bush administration, said he had never seen the agency publicly disavow responsibility for a rule it was publishing and responsible for enforcing. Only the Commerce Department has the technical expertise or legal authority to write such a rule, he said, but the statement made clear that the agency did not want to issue the rule and did so under duress.

It’s “like open mutiny,” Mr. Padilla said. “That’s unprecedented, and publicly signals a breakdown of interagency cooperation. Not a great signal to send anytime, but especially on the eve of a summit meeting.”

Officials have had limited expectations for the China meetings, which are likely to touch on trade, nuclear weapons and the war in Iran.

In a briefing call on Friday night, administration officials said they did not expect to reach an agreement on nuclear nonproliferation at the summit. They said that the focus of meetings with Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader, and other Chinese officials would be implementing a trade agreement between Washington and Beijing. That would include reducing tariffs and other barriers to trade on each side, and ensuring that China was supplying the United States with rare earth minerals.

In a speech at the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations gala last week, Mr. Bessent said that he was working with his Chinese counterparts to establish an alert system so that the countries could notify each other of serious incidents involving A.I. models. Despite his more hawkish tone, Mr. Bessent said that he did not want to sever economic ties with China.

“As we work toward a more balanced relationship, our objective is to de-risk, not to decouple,” Mr. Bessent said.

For now, Mr. Trump is not publicly taking sides in the rivalry between Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick.

“One view is, you don’t want to insult China,” Mr. Trump said on Monday as he departed for his trip. “The other view is, just go down and dirty and do what you have to do. You can’t say either is wrong or right.”

He added: “I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there.”

Tony Romm contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Government Demand for LinkedIn Data Was Over Times Reporters’ Sources
item.description:
The Trump administration sought to force LinkedIn to turn over data about New York Times reporters as part of a leak investigation into a 2025 article about a failed top secret mission in North Korea, according to a court filing unsealed on Monday.

Federal prosecutors made the disclosure in recent days to lawyers for Matthew Cole, a freelancer who helped write the article, which described the botched operation by Navy SEALs in 2019.

The court filing confirms that the Trump administration has sought on two parallel fronts to identify the sources for the article as part of one overarching investigation. The administration subpoenaed Mr. Cole in February to testify about two years’ worth of information about his contacts and conversations. Lawyers for Mr. Cole have been trying to quash the subpoena as an impermissible intrusion on the First Amendment.

The rising pressure on journalists adds to the Trump administration’s increasingly aggressive efforts to investigate leaks, a top priority of the president and his senior aides. This year, the Justice Department has subpoenaed reporters at multiple news outlets, searched the home of a Washington Post reporter and contemplated naming The Times as a conspirator in another leak case.

In the investigation related to Mr. Cole’s reporting, prosecutors told his lawyer, David O’Neil, that they had demanded that LinkedIn share metadata from his client’s account, according to the court filing. According to lawyers’ statements in court, prosecutors sought the LinkedIn data for six different accounts — an indication that they are looking at the digital activities of Mr. Cole, the four other Times journalists whose names appeared on the article, and one other person who may not be a reporter. The prosecutors also sought Mr. Cole’s phone records — data showing whom he called and received calls from, and how long they spoke.

“These are the two efforts in this investigation to obtain records from third parties related to Mr. Cole,” the prosecutors told his lawyer, according to the court filing.

In a statement, a spokesman for The New York Times, Charlie Stadtlander, said the disclosure suggested that the Justice Department was not following its own rules for conducting leak investigations. “This is another troubling example of the Justice Department violating the law, precedent and even its own guidelines by attempting to extract information from journalists and their communications providers,” he said. “It is an affront to the legal rights protecting a free press.”

Mr. Cole is now seeking to delay a hearing scheduled for Thursday over a grand jury subpoena to try to force him to testify about his sources. He is arguing that there are too many legal and factual uncertainties after an appeals court ruled against the administration last week in its effort to obtain 18 months of data from LinkedIn.

A three-judge panel halted a lower-court order requiring LinkedIn to give the Trump administration such an extensive trove of private data, saying that it could reveal the identities of numerous unrelated confidential sources.

The Trump administration has indicated that it may appeal that ruling, and Mr. O’Neil, in court papers, argued that until the LinkedIn case was resolved, “Mr. Cole — and this court — likely lack the full picture of the investigative steps (and the legitimacy of such steps) the government has taken to pursue its investigation and the nature of any violations of its internal regulations.”

Prosecutors oppose any delay, noting that a magistrate judge had already recommended that Mr. Cole be required to testify about his sources, and that it could take a long time to resolve the LinkedIn matter.

The prosecutors’ filing also argued that there was nothing improper or punitive about the subpoena, and that Mr. Cole “has never been threatened with jail by any representative of the United States for refusing to testify in response to a grand jury subpoena.”

Jon Palmer, the chief legal officer of Microsoft, the parent company of LinkedIn, wrote last week that the company had a responsibility to its users and to following the law. “When users are unaware that the government is seeking their information, technology providers are the last line of defense,” he said.

The Trump administration had pursued the LinkedIn data largely in secret, imposing a gag order to shield it from public view and preventing the company from disclosing the government’s efforts. The company went to court to object to the extent of the data demand and the gag order.

Writing for a unanimous three-judge panel, Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III, an appointee of President Ronald Reagan, stressed the importance of First Amendment press freedoms.

“A request by the government to scoop up reporters’ records wholesale and ascertain the identity of their sources would tip the balance against informed discourse in a manner inimical to democratic health,” he wrote. “It is important not to view the value of a free press in isolation. Press freedom is among those things viewed by autocrats worldwide as a threat to their grip on power.”

The article by Mr. Cole and a Times reporter recounted how a Navy SEAL Team 6 unit slipped into North Korean territory at night to plant a surveillance device. Interrupted by a boat, the troops feared they had been discovered by security forces, and shot and killed everyone aboard. The North Koreans turned out to be unarmed civilians. The first Trump administration did not inform Congress of the operation.

Mr. Cole has also written a book, “Princes and Thieves,” about the finances and global entanglements of President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

item.title: What Pete Buttigieg’s Bet in 2026 Could Mean for 2028
item.description:
Not long after Jamie Ager, a farmer in Western North Carolina and a Democrat, announced a long-shot run for Congress, his phone rang. Pete Buttigieg was on the line, offering to help.

It was the summer of 2025, long before national Democrats realized they had a shot at winning districts like Ager’s, which President Trump carried by nearly 10 percentage points in 2024. But it was exactly the kind of place Buttigieg wanted to plant a flag — and Ager’s campaign was happy to have him, even as it kept its distance from most national Democrats.

“People don’t hate him,” Grayson Barnette, Ager’s campaign manager, said. “Right?”

The 2026 midterms were not exactly primed to be the Year of Pete. He passed on running for Senate in Michigan. His association with the Biden administration, in which he served for four years as transportation secretary, was hardly a boon in a party desperate to move on. He was neither a governor nor a member of Congress with a built-in platform.

But seven years after Buttigieg, then the mayor of South Bend, Ind., made himself an unavoidable fixture of Democratic politics by running in the 2020 presidential election, he made himself an unavoidable fixture of the midterm campaign trail. He campaigned for more than 100 candidates in person, often in traditionally conservative states like Oklahoma, Kansas, Texas and Mississippi. He felt his party was too quick to pass over such places — and believed Trump’s unpopularity had handed Democrats an unusual opportunity in them.

Those ventures could give Buttigieg new allies as he considers a second presidential run, a decision he will make early next year, according to a person familiar with his thinking. And the results, which included a victory for Ager, have set him up to argue that what a party dazzled by progressives and fresher faces really needs is a moderate red-state whisperer like himself.

“The broader mistake I was worried about the party making was not paying enough attention to these redder areas, which is why I made a point of paying a lot of attention to them,” Buttigieg said in an interview.

Buttigieg was also a fixture of last weekend’s gathering of Democrats in Denver, where he spoke on the main stage, popped up at one happy hour after another, and appraised the performance of the current transportation secretary in real time as flights ground to a halt across the nation.

I spoke with Buttigieg twice in recent months, curious about his unusual midterm strategy — and the unsubtle signals it sent about his ambitions for 2028.

David Axelrod, a Democratic strategist who described himself as a friend and admirer of Buttigieg’s, told me that building relationships across the country was valuable in a presidential primary, when there are delegates to be won everywhere. A successful candidate needs to be able to tell a story about the country, he said, and Buttigieg can do that.

“Obviously, he’s not the shiny new thing anymore,” Axelrod said. “I was thinking about that when I watched him speak in Denver, his hair flecked with gray and his graying beard.”

Now, there will be “other shiny new objects in this field,” Axelrod noted. “That is a challenge.”

The primaries minted newer, edgier stars like Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic senator-elect. In the closing weeks of the campaign, the surrogate who drew the most national attention, aside from former President Barack Obama, was probably Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Even the lane of expand-the-map Democrats is crowded with potential 2028 candidates like Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky, who spent the night before the election in Oklahoma, as well as Black Democrats like Senator Raphael Warnock who believe their party needs to embark on a long-term effort to build its strength in the South.

Buttigieg, who has not held elected office since he retired as mayor on New Year’s Day in 2020, said it was not a problem that his party is teeming with talent.

“I think the more the merrier,” he said. “We’ve got a lot of great leaders emerging in the party. As somebody who came out of nowhere eight years ago, I think that’s a good thing.”

And he insisted that attention lavished on progressives was not a sign of an intractable divide within the party.

“The candidates who’ve done best are focusing on these everyday-life issues, regardless of whether the commentators prefer to label them as centrists or leftists,” he said. All Democrats, he said, wanted to make health care more affordable, raise people’s pay, end the war in Iran and reverse Trump’s cuts to the social safety net.

“These are things that unite 99 percent of the Democratic Party and two-thirds of the American people,” Buttigieg said. “That ought to be our center of gravity.”

Party chairs in states like Kansas and Oklahoma welcomed Buttigieg this year. They saw him as a cheerleader who could draw a crowd and amp up Democrats without putting off moderates and independent voters. And he has found his travels encouraging as he weighs the decision of whether or not to run.

The campaign for Scott Colom, whose narrow victory over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith will make him the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction, asked Buttigieg to appear with him there, so the two could talk about infrastructure funding. Buttigieg appeared in Iowa with Josh Turek, the state’s new senator-elect, and in Louisiana with Jamie Davis, who came close to beating a Republican in that state’s Senate race.

“It was a chance to say to observers, to commentators, to the national party itself, but most importantly to these communities, that I believed in them, and I believe that they could elect great Democrats,” Buttigieg said.

It was also a chance for Buttigieg to build out his national network — and to campaign both on behalf of Black candidates and in states like South Carolina, where Black voters will shape early primary contests in 2028. His presidential campaign in 2020 was unable to gain traction with Black voters, who overwhelmingly supported Joe Biden.

“It’s critically important to come into the state and be comfortable doing small gatherings,” Christale Spain, the chair of the South Carolina Democratic Party, told me. Buttigieg was the featured speaker at a conference the party held in the state in late August.

In a sign of his continued interest in South Carolina, he called Spain after the election to congratulate her on the party’s successes there, which included the unexpected victory of the Democrat Annie Andrews in the Senate race there.

On the trail, he has sought to present his time in the Biden administration as an asset, talking up nuts-and-bolts infrastructure investments he pushed for as secretary of transportation. He presents as older and wiser, making crowds laugh with stories of his twins’ chaotic soccer practice and comments about his age (now 44).

His family has been a target, too, after an anonymous “swatting” report caused social services to separate him from his twins for 24 hours. He said the episode had shaped his thinking about the personal cost of participating in politics.

“It’s really motivated me to make sure that I’m doing my part to build a kind of politics where, even when we don’t agree on the issues, we agree on the boundaries,” Buttigieg said.

I’m planning to speak with more potential 2028 presidential candidates. Tell me who you want to hear from at onpolitics@nytimes.com.

catch me up

The Trump administration said it was moving forward with a rule that would clamp down on China’s access to advanced A.I. chips.

That move comes ahead of the president’s trip to China this week, which will be the first time Trump has sat down with President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir Putin of Russia at the same time.

As he prepared for the visit, the president played down the fallout from Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman whom officials have identified as an intelligence asset for Beijing.

Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland contended that he had a “wide-open” path to unseat Chuck Schumer, the long-serving Senate Democratic leader — who, for his part, says there is no path.

After their midterm triumph, Democrats are eagerly looking ahead to 2028. Read my colleagues’ dispatch on the (very) early jockeying.

A Democrat has won the governor’s race in Alaska for the first time since 1988. The Senate race there is still uncalled, but the Democrat, former Representative Mary Peltola, has a narrow lead.

In One Graphic

Democrats have been fiercely debating for nearly a decade whether the party should move to the left or the center. This month’s midterm results were almost perfectly calibrated to make sure the debate rages into the next presidential primary.

That’s because progressive candidates underperformed by enough and in enough races to keep the old “electability” debate alive and well, The Times’s Nate Cohn writes. Read more here.

In the states

Democrats in six states — Arizona, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Nevada, Michigan and Minnesota — have netted a new “trifecta,” or one-party control of the governor’s office and both chambers of the legislature.

The Times talked to Democratic leaders from these states about their plans:

Democrats here plan to quickly enact laws that would increase transit funding, more than double the minimum wage and allow people to seek civil damages for childhood sexual abuse, among other measures.

Democrats in Wisconsin say they plan to move swiftly after more than a decade and a half of at least partial Republican control of state government. Greta Neubauer, the incoming Assembly speaker, said she and fellow Democrats hoped to address affordability by lowering the costs of groceries, gas, health care and child care.

In Arizona, Democrats are likely to use their majorities to repeal abortion restrictions, increase funding for public schools and further protect the state’s dwindling supply of groundwater.

Gov. Katie Hobbs marveled at how 15 years ago, there were so few Democrats in the Legislature there that a single pizza could feed them all. Now, she said, “We’re going to need a lot more pizzas.”

Read what’s happening in the other states.

ONE LAST THING

In the aftermath of the midterms, Joe Rogan had more to say about hominids and dinosaurs than politics.

But on Friday, he offered a harsh assessment of Trump’s policies, after endorsing him in 2024. He said support for Trump had frayed because of the war in Iran — which he described as a conflict “no one wants to be in” — and because of the immigration crackdown.

“They didn’t just lose the podcast bros,” Rogan said. “They lost most of the country.”

Read more here.

Taylor Robinson contributed reporting.
